highlights.quote: Nataruk is a place where violence became archaeologically visible. It is not a census of every encounter that occurred around Lake Turkana.
highlights.judgment: Strength: the book's governing distinction — capability versus prevalence — stated with exemplary economy.

highlights.quote: A wall is not a battle report. A weapon is not a record of its use. A scar is not a statement of motive.
highlights.judgment: Strength of thought, weakness of form: genuinely clarifying, but the tripled negative parallelism is the book's most overused rhetorical gear.
Strength: a rare short, concrete sentence that does more argumentative work than the paragraphs around it.

highlights.quote: A compensation rule is not a compensation payment.
highlights.judgment: Strength: precise, memorable, and earns the long discussion of Hammurabi's silver tariffs that precedes it.

highlights.quote: The denominator is not a technical afterthought; it determines which social pattern becomes visible.
highlights.judgment: Strength: the methodological core of chapter 13, and one of the few places the book's abstraction pays an obvious dividend.

highlights.quote: Law did not make force disappear. It made some force official.
highlights.judgment: Weakness in aggregate: an effective line, but nearly every chapter lands on a paired antithesis of exactly this shape.

highlights.quote: The body supplies possibilities, the mind interprets occasions, and the social world decides which possibilities become ordinary, useful, forbidden, or celebrated.
highlights.judgment: Weakness: an aphoristic triadic closer that restates the chapter rather than advancing it; the same cadence closes chapters 1, 2, 6, 10 and 12.

highlights.quote: The record is sharpest where lives were broken and quietest where people succeeded in preventing the break.
highlights.judgment: Weakness: elegant but decorative — the chiastic closer substitutes symmetry for a new claim.

recurringPatterns.pattern: The symmetrical can-show / cannot-show hedge, applied to virtually every case in the book, so that each section ends by retracting most of what it advanced. Used once it is rigour; used several times per chapter across fourteen chapters it becomes the book's default paragraph engine and its chief source of redundancy.
instances: It cannot establish the prevalence of warfare among foragers
What it cannot show is equally important.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Definitional antithesis in the form "X is not A; it is B" or "not merely A but B," used to open or close nearly every analytical move rather than reserved for genuinely contested definitions.
instances: Universal equality before law was not the code
Enforcement is therefore not a technical afterthought. It determines whether a rule enters the chain of decision.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Long undifferentiated catalogues of occupations, offices or materials used as a substitute for describing one of them concretely; the lists recur in the Kadesh, Assyrian, Wannsee, Sarajevo and camp chapters with interchangeable rhythm.
instances: Chariot makers, grooms, smiths, drivers, armourers, road builders, scribes, cooks, porters, scouts, and local guides formed the practical body of the army.
Officials had to identify people, assemble them, guard them, provision them, move them across long distances, allocate land or labour, and record their new status.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Aphoristic, balanced closers that summarise rather than extend, ending sections on a cadence of paired or tripled clauses instead of on a new consequence.
instances: Law did not make force disappear. It made some force official.
The record is sharpest where lives were broken and quietest where people succeeded in preventing the break.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Substantive duplication across chapters: the Nuremberg Laws and Wannsee Protocol are narrated at length twice (chapters 8 and 12), and Nataruk is re-described in chapters 1, 2, 13 and 14 with much of the same evidentiary detail, so the last two chapters read largely as recapitulation.
instances: The First Regulation to the Reich Citizenship Law, issued in November 1935, defined a Jew generally as someone descended from at least three Jewish grandparents.
The November regulations defined Jewishness through the religious affiliation of grandparents and the status of parents, not simply through a person

summary: This is a genuinely coherent book with a real and unusual thesis: that the history of violence is a history of what different classes of evidence — bones, weapons, settlements, law codes, royal annals, ethnography, homicide series, testimony — can and cannot support, and that capacity, frequency and organisation must never be conflated. The argumentative discipline is the strongest thing here; from Nataruk through Hammurabi, Kadesh, the Twelve Tables, Nuremberg, Sarajevo and the South African commission, inferences are calibrated to their sources with a care most trade history lacks, and the closing chapters on denominators, negative cases and mechanism-versus-law are genuinely instructive. The cost is severe. The book has one rhetorical move — assert what the evidence shows, then symmetrically retract what it does not — and performs it hundreds of times, so pacing flatlines and paragraphs become interchangeable in shape; chapter 12 re-narrates chapter 8's documents, and chapters 13 and 14 largely re-narrate everything. Voice is uniform, impersonal and abstract, with almost no scene, person or image sustained long enough to grip a reader, and the prose leans on nominalisation and on balanced antitheses and triads that read as manufactured cadence rather than thought. Surface AI tells are largely absent, but the structural templating — paired negations, catalogue lists, aphoristic closers — is pervasive enough to register as medium slop. With aggressive cutting of the retraction formula, elimination of the duplicated Holocaust and Nataruk material, and a deliberate variation of tempo and register, this could be a distinguished book; as it stands it needs moderate revision.
